package_info.why_malicious: The package was backdoored at the vendor level, introducing a malicious DLL (nssock2.dll) that enabled remote access and control by attackers. This allowed adversaries to compromise any organization that installed the affected update, providing a covert foothold and data exfiltration capabilities.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when the DLL is loaded by the NetSarang application process
execution_context.file_location: nssock2.dll (within the NetSarang software installation directory)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: ShadowPad backdoor code (Win32.Trojan.Shadowpad) embedded in nssock2.dll, as detected by AV engines and behavioral analysis.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code establishes a covert outbound connection to a remote command and control server, receives and executes attacker-supplied commands on the host system, and exfiltrates sensitive data via the established channel, resulting in persistent unauthorized remote access and data theft.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The DLL contains additional code not present in the legitimate version, which initiates outbound network connections to attacker-controlled infrastructure and enables remote command execution and data exfiltration.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate network library DLL should only provide documented networking functionality and should not initiate unsolicited outbound connections or execute arbitrary remote commands.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote administration tools may have similar capabilities, but only with explicit user consent, proper authentication, and clear documentation of such features.
key_indicators: Presence of network beaconing and command-and-control (C2) communication routines within the DLL
Ability to execute arbitrary commands received from a remote server
Detection as Win32.Trojan.Shadowpad by multiple antivirus engines
Code sections and behaviors not present in previous known-good versions of nssock2.dll
Outbound connections to domains or IPs associated with ShadowPad C2 infrastructure

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when the Android app is installed and the user grants requested permissions
execution_context.file_location: Exodus APK (Android app package, installed on device)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Android.Trojan.Exod code requesting camera, location, microphone, networking, and SMS read permissions.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code accesses the device's camera, microphone, and location services, reads SMS messages, and transmits the collected sensitive data to a remote server over the network, resulting in unauthorized surveillance and data exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The app requests a broad set of highly sensitive permissions that are not justified by its stated functionality, and combines extensive data collection with covert network exfiltration to remote servers.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate apps should only request permissions necessary for their core function, and should not silently collect and transmit sensitive user data without clear user awareness and consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Parental control or enterprise monitoring apps may request similar permissions, but only with explicit user consent, transparent disclosure, and secure handling of collected data.
key_indicators: Unjustified access to camera, microphone, and location services
Network exfiltration of sensitive data (photos, audio, location, SMS)
Detection as Android.Trojan.Exod by multiple antivirus engines
Suspicious combination of permissions (read SMS + internet + camera + microphone)
Outbound connections to remote servers not associated with legitimate app functionality

attack_chain.action: Attacker compromises the software vendor's build or update process and injects a malicious DLL (ShadowPad) into the distributed package.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious DLL is distributed to and installed by downstream organizations.

attack_chain.action: Victim organization installs the compromised software update, loading the malicious DLL into the application process.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code executes on victim systems.

attack_chain.action: Malicious DLL establishes a covert channel to the attacker's command and control (C2) server, enabling remote command execution and data exfiltration.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains persistent access and can steal sensitive data from compromised systems.

attack_chain.action: In the case of mobile supply chain attacks (e.g., Exodus), the malicious app is distributed via a trusted app store, installed by users, and abuses permissions to exfiltrate data.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives sensitive user data from infected devices.

behavioral_signatures: Unexpected outbound network connections initiated by DLLs or app components not documented to require such behavior
Execution of arbitrary commands received from remote servers by software components not intended for remote administration
Access to sensitive device features (camera, microphone, location) without clear functional justification or user notification
Combination of sensitive data collection and network exfiltration in applications not designed for security or monitoring purposes
file_indicators: Presence of nssock2.dll with SHA1 hash f1a181d29b38dfe60d8ea487e8ed0ef30f064763 in NetSarang software installations
Android APKs requesting camera, microphone, location, and SMS read permissions together, especially when not justified by app description
Unexpected changes in file size, code sections, or capabilities between software versions (e.g., new network routines in DLLs)
network_indicators: Outbound connections from nssock2.dll to known ShadowPad C2 domains or IP addresses
Android apps establishing connections to suspicious or unlisted remote servers for data exfiltration
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Continuously monitor for unexpected network activity from software components, such as DLLs initiating outbound connections or apps transmitting sensitive data. Compare new software versions against known-good baselines to identify added capabilities or suspicious indicators. Flag apps or packages that request excessive or unusual combinations of permissions, or that exhibit both sensitive data access and network communication. Use automated static and behavioral analysis tools (e.g., ReversingLabs A1000) to scan and compare software updates before deployment, and correlate file hashes, permission requests, and network destinations with known IOCs.
